items.readable_text:
Content:
A first-order linear homogeneous recurrence relation is a recurrence relation that takes the form

Content:
[MATH: a_n + P \cdot a_{n-1} = 0]

Content:
where [MATH: P] is a nonzero constant.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following first-order recurrence relation:

Content:
[MATH: a_n -2 a_{n-1}= 0]

Content:
This equation is first-order homogeneous because the left-hand is a linear combination of [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n-1},] and the right-hand side is zero.

Content:
A first-order linear inhomogeneous recurrence relation is a recurrence relation that can be written as

Content:
[MATH: a_n + P \cdot a_{n-1} = f(n).]

Content:
The function [MATH: f(n)] is sometimes called a forcing function.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following first-order recurrence relation:

Content:
[MATH: a_n -2 a_{n-1}= 2^n]

Content:
This equation is inhomogeneous because the right-hand side is [MATH: f(n) = 2^n,] which is different from zero.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to find the generating function for the sequence satisfying the inhomogeneous recurrence relation

Content:
[MATH: a_n-2a_{n-1}=2, \qquad a_0=1, \qquad n \ge 1.]

Content:
Since the equation is inhomogeneous, the method we used in the homogeneous case will not work. However, we can still find a closed-form solution.

Content:
Let's suppose that the generating function of our sequence is

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.]

Content:
Next, we multiply both sides of the recurrence relation by [MATH: x^n.] This gives

Content:
[MATH: a_nx^n -2a_{n−1}x^n =2 x^n.]

Content:
Now, if we sum this equation over all values of [MATH: n \geq 1,] we get

Content:
[MATH: \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n - \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2a_{n−1}x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2 x^n.\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
The idea now is to write each of the summations in equation [MATH: (\ast)] terms of [MATH: f(x).]

Content:
- The first sum on the left-hand side is almost the same as [MATH: f(x).] It's just missing the first term. Therefore,
[MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n - a_0 = f(x) - 1.]
- The second sum on the left-hand side has a mismatch between the indexes. To correct this, we can pull a single factor of [MATH: x] outside the sum:
[MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2a_{n−1}x^n = 2x \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^{n-1} = 2x \left( a_0x^0 + a_1x^1 + a_2x^2 + \cdots \right)]
Now, we can start the index from zero, which gives
[MATH: 2x \left( a_0x^0 + a_1x^1 + a_2x^2 + \cdots \right) = 2x \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_{n}x^n = 2x f(x).]
- The sum on the right-hand side can be evaluated as geometric series:
[MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2 x^n = 2x\sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty x^{n-1} = 2x\sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty x^n= \dfrac{2x}{1-x}]

Content:
Therefore, the equation [MATH: (\ast)] can be rewritten as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (f(x) − 1) − 2xf(x)|= (2x)/(1 − x); f(x)(1 − 2x) − 1|= (2x)/(1 − x); f(x)(1 − 2x)|= (2x)/(1 − x) + 1; f(x)(1 − 2x)|= (1 + x)/(1 − x); f(x)|= (1 + x)/((1 − x)(1 − 2x))]

sections.normalized_html: Find the generating function for the sequence that satisfies the recurrence relation [MATH: a_n + 4a_{n−1}=(-2)^n] with [MATH: a_0=1.]
sections.readable_text: Find the generating function for the sequence that satisfies the recurrence relation [MATH: a_n + 4a_{n−1}=(-2)^n] with [MATH: a_0=1.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's denote the generating function of our sequence as

[MATH: f(x) = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.]

We start by multiplying both sides of the recurrence relation by [MATH: x^n.] This gives

[MATH: a_n x^n + 4a_{n−1}x^n = (-2)^n x^n.]

If we sum this over all values of [MATH: n \geq 1,] we get

[MATH: \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n + \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 4a_{n−1}x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (-2)^n x^n.]

Now, notice the following:

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n - a_0 = f(x) - 1]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 4a_{n−1}x^n = 4x \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^{n-1} = 4x \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n = 4x f(x)]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (-2)^n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (-2x)^n = \dfrac{-2x}{1-(-2x)} = -\dfrac{2x}{1+2x}]

Therefore, our equation can be rewritten as follows:

[MATH: (f(x) − 1) + 4xf(x)|= − (2x)/(1 + 2x); f(x)(1 + 4x) − 1|= − (2x)/(1 + 2x); f(x)(1 + 4x)|= 1 − (2x)/(1 + 2x); f(x)(1 + 4x)|= (1)/(1 + 2x); f(x)|= (1)/((1 + 2x)(1 + 4x))]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's denote the generating function of our sequence as

[MATH: f(x) = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.]

We start by multiplying both sides of the recurrence relation by [MATH: x^n.] This gives

[MATH: a_nx^n -a_{n−1}x^n =(1-3n) x^n.]

If we sum this over all values of [MATH: n \geq 1,] we get

[MATH: \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n - \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (1-3n) x^n.]

Now, notice the following:

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n - a_0 = f(x) - 2]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^n = x \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^{n-1} = x \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_{n}x^n = x f(x)]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (1-3n) x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty x^n -3 \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty n x^n = \dfrac{x}{1-x}-\dfrac{3x}{(1-x)^2}]

Therefore, our equation can be rewritten as follows:

[MATH: (f(x) − 2) − xf(x)|= (x)/(1 − x) − (3x)/((1 − x)^{2}); f(x)(1 − x) − 2|= (− 2x − x^{2})/((1 − x)^{2}); f(x)(1 − x)|= (− 2x − x^{2})/((1 − x)^{2}) + 2; f(x)(1 − x)|= (x^{2} − 6x + 2)/((1 − x)^{2}); f(x)|= (x^{2} − 6x + 2)/((1 − x)^{3})]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A first-order linear homogeneous recurrence relation is a recurrence relation that takes the form

Content:
[MATH: a_n + P \cdot a_{n-1} = 0]

Content:
where [MATH: P] is a nonzero constant.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following first-order recurrence relation:

Content:
[MATH: a_n -2 a_{n-1}= 0]

Content:
This equation is first-order homogeneous because the left-hand is a linear combination of [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n-1},] and the right-hand side is zero.

Content:
A first-order linear inhomogeneous recurrence relation is a recurrence relation that can be written as

Content:
[MATH: a_n + P \cdot a_{n-1} = f(n).]

Content:
The function [MATH: f(n)] is sometimes called a forcing function.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following first-order recurrence relation:

Content:
[MATH: a_n -2 a_{n-1}= 2^n]

Content:
This equation is inhomogeneous because the right-hand side is [MATH: f(n) = 2^n,] which is different from zero.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Generating Functions for Inhomogeneous Recurrence Relations

Content:
Suppose we want to find the generating function for the sequence satisfying the inhomogeneous recurrence relation

Content:
[MATH: a_n-2a_{n-1}=2, \qquad a_0=1, \qquad n \ge 1.]

Content:
Since the equation is inhomogeneous, the method we used in the homogeneous case will not work. However, we can still find a closed-form solution.

Content:
Let's suppose that the generating function of our sequence is

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.]

Content:
Next, we multiply both sides of the recurrence relation by [MATH: x^n.] This gives

Content:
[MATH: a_nx^n -2a_{n−1}x^n =2 x^n.]

Content:
Now, if we sum this equation over all values of [MATH: n \geq 1,] we get

Content:
[MATH: \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n - \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2a_{n−1}x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2 x^n.\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
The idea now is to write each of the summations in equation [MATH: (\ast)] terms of [MATH: f(x).]

Content:
- The first sum on the left-hand side is almost the same as [MATH: f(x).] It's just missing the first term. Therefore,
[MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n - a_0 = f(x) - 1.]
- The second sum on the left-hand side has a mismatch between the indexes. To correct this, we can pull a single factor of [MATH: x] outside the sum:
[MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2a_{n−1}x^n = 2x \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^{n-1} = 2x \left( a_0x^0 + a_1x^1 + a_2x^2 + \cdots \right)]
Now, we can start the index from zero, which gives
[MATH: 2x \left( a_0x^0 + a_1x^1 + a_2x^2 + \cdots \right) = 2x \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_{n}x^n = 2x f(x).]
- The sum on the right-hand side can be evaluated as geometric series:
[MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 2 x^n = 2x\sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty x^{n-1} = 2x\sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty x^n= \dfrac{2x}{1-x}]

Content:
Therefore, the equation [MATH: (\ast)] can be rewritten as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (f(x) − 1) − 2xf(x)|= (2x)/(1 − x); f(x)(1 − 2x) − 1|= (2x)/(1 − x); f(x)(1 − 2x)|= (2x)/(1 − x) + 1; f(x)(1 − 2x)|= (1 + x)/(1 − x); f(x)|= (1 + x)/((1 − x)(1 − 2x))]

---

Item 3 — Example: First-Order Inhomogeneous Recurrence Relations With Constant or Exponential Forcing

Example Prompt:
Find the generating function for the sequence that satisfies the recurrence relation [MATH: a_n + 4a_{n−1}=(-2)^n] with [MATH: a_0=1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's denote the generating function of our sequence as

[MATH: f(x) = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.]

We start by multiplying both sides of the recurrence relation by [MATH: x^n.] This gives

[MATH: a_n x^n + 4a_{n−1}x^n = (-2)^n x^n.]

If we sum this over all values of [MATH: n \geq 1,] we get

[MATH: \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n + \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 4a_{n−1}x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (-2)^n x^n.]

Now, notice the following:

- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n - a_0 = f(x) - 1]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty 4a_{n−1}x^n = 4x \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^{n-1} = 4x \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n = 4x f(x)]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (-2)^n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (-2x)^n = \dfrac{-2x}{1-(-2x)} = -\dfrac{2x}{1+2x}]

Therefore, our equation can be rewritten as follows:

[MATH: (f(x) − 1) + 4xf(x)|= − (2x)/(1 + 2x); f(x)(1 + 4x) − 1|= − (2x)/(1 + 2x); f(x)(1 + 4x)|= 1 − (2x)/(1 + 2x); f(x)(1 + 4x)|= (1)/(1 + 2x); f(x)|= (1)/((1 + 2x)(1 + 4x))]

---

[MATH: a_nx^n -a_{n−1}x^n =(1-3n) x^n.]

[MATH: \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n - \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (1-3n) x^n.]

Now, notice the following:

- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n - a_0 = f(x) - 2]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^n = x \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty a_{n−1}x^{n-1} = x \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty a_{n}x^n = x f(x)]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty (1-3n) x^n = \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty x^n -3 \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty n x^n = \dfrac{x}{1-x}-\dfrac{3x}{(1-x)^2}]

Therefore, our equation can be rewritten as follows:

[MATH: (f(x) − 2) − xf(x)|= (x)/(1 − x) − (3x)/((1 − x)^{2}); f(x)(1 − x) − 2|= (− 2x − x^{2})/((1 − x)^{2}); f(x)(1 − x)|= (− 2x − x^{2})/((1 − x)^{2}) + 2; f(x)(1 − x)|= (x^{2} − 6x + 2)/((1 − x)^{2}); f(x)|= (x^{2} − 6x + 2)/((1 − x)^{3})]
